dervis-irab:1-11.t:
* Vocabulary:
(الْعادِياتِ) The horses that run swiftly on a raid; the yāʾ is from a wāw because of the kasra before it.
(ضَبْحاً) It is the sound of their chests. In al-Mukhtār: "Ḍabaḥat al-khayl, of the pattern qaṭaʿa; al-ḍabḥ is the sound of their breaths when they run." In al-Qāmūs: "Ḍabaḥat al-khayl ḍabḥan and ḍabāḥan: they made a sound audible from their mouths that is neither neighing nor snorting; or they ran at less than a trot." Al-Farrāʾ said: "Al-ḍabḥ is the sound of horses when they run. Ibn ʿAbbās said: no animal makes the ḍabḥ except the horse, the dog and the fox. It was also said that they were muzzled so as not to neigh and let the enemy know of them, so in that state they breathed forcefully; these animals make the ḍabḥ only when their state changes from fright or fatigue." In al-Qāmūs: "Kaʿamtu l-baʿīr, like manaʿa, so it is makʿūm and kaʿīm: I tied its mouth shut so that it would not bite or eat; and what it is muzzled with is called kiʿām, like kitāb." Al-Zamakhsharī said: "He swears by the horses of the raiders, which run and pant. Al-ḍabḥ is the sound of their breaths when they run. It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that he imitated it, saying: 'aḥ, aḥ.' ʿAntara said:
والخيل تكدح حين تضب ... ح في حياض الموت ضبحا
(And the horses strain hard when they pant, in the pools of death, panting.)"
Al-kadḥ is earnest effort in running; ʿAntara compared death to a torrent by way of implicit metaphor (istiʿāra makniyya), and "pools" is its imaginative embellishment (takhyīl).
(فَالْمُورِياتِ) The horses that strike fire with their hooves, i.e., strike sparks, as the fire-stick strikes fire; this is the fire of al-Ḥubāḥib. The maṣdar is awrā yūrī īrāʾan, so it is mūrin. Al-Nābigha said:
تقد السلوقي المضاعف نسجه ... وتوقد بالصفاح نار الحباحب
(She cuts through the Salūqī mail of doubled weave, and strikes with the flat stones the fire of al-Ḥubāḥib.)
Al-Ḥubāḥib, as in al-Ṣiḥāḥ, is the name of a miserly man who would light only a weak fire for fear of guests; so they made him a proverb, until they said "the fire of al-Ḥubāḥib" for what horses strike out with their hooves.
In al-Miṣbāḥ: "Warā l-zand yarī, of the pattern waʿada, and in one dialect wariya yariy, with kasra on both; and awrā, with alif, which is when it brings out its fire." In al-Mukhtār: "And someone else awrāhu." It is learned from what is in al-Miṣbāḥ and al-Mukhtār that it is used as a triliteral intransitive and as a quadriliteral both intransitive and transitive; and what is in the verse is of the transitive quadriliteral type.
(قَدْحاً) A maṣdar of qadaḥa; one says qadaḥtu l-ḥajar bi-l-ḥajar, i.e., I struck one against the other. The original sense of al-qadḥ is extraction, hence qadaḥtu l-ʿayn when you drain the bad water out of it; iqtadaḥtu l-zand; iqtadaḥtu l-maraq, I ladled it out. Al-miqdaḥa, with kasra on the mīm, is what fire is struck with; al-qaddāḥa and al-qaddāḥ are the stone that gives fire.
(فَالْمُغِيراتِ) The horses that raid the enemy. In al-Miṣbāḥ: "Aghāra l-faras ighāratan, the noun being al-ghāra, like aṭāʿa iṭāʿatan, the noun being al-ṭāʿa: when it hastens in running; and aghāra l-qawm ighāratan: they hastened in marching." In al-Qāmūs: "Aghāra ʿalā l-qawm ghāratan and ighāratan: he drove the horses at them; aghāra l-faras: its running grew intense, in a raid or otherwise." He said:
أغار على العدو بكل طرف ... وسلهبة تجول بلا حزام
(He raided the enemy with every noble steed and tall mare that roams without a girth.)
(فَأَثَرْنَ) They stirred up. One says thāra yathūru thawran, thawarānan and thuʾūran: it was stirred; hence thārat al-fitna baynahum, strife broke out among them; thāra l-ghubār or the smoke: it rose; thāra l-jarād: the locusts appeared; thārat nafsuhu: he retched; thāra ilayhi and bihi: he leapt upon him.
(نَقْعاً) Dust. Al-naqʿ is also that a person quenches his thirst by drinking water; one says naqaʿtu ghullī bi-sharba mā'. Bashshār said:
كأن مثار النقع فوق رؤوسنا ... وأسيافنا ليل تهاوى كواكبه
(As if the rising dust above our heads, with our swords, were a night whose stars come tumbling down.)
(فَوَسَطْنَ) They came into the middle. In al-Miṣbāḥ: "One says wasaṭtu l-qawm and the place, asiṭu wasṭan, of the pattern waʿada, when you came into the middle of it; the agent is wāsiṭ, and from it the famous town in Iraq was named, because it lies in the middle of the region." In al-Mukhtār: you say jalastu wasṭa l-qawm with sukūn, because it is an adverb, and jalastu wasaṭa l-dār with vowelled middle, because it is a noun for what is surrounded by other things on its sides; every place where "between" is suitable is wasṭ with sukūn, and where "between" is not suitable it is wasaṭ with vowel, though sometimes it is given sukūn, which is not the preferred form.
The wording of al-Qāmūs: "Wasaṭahum, like waʿada, wasṭan and wasṭatan: he sat among them, like tawassaṭahum; he is wasīṭ among them, i.e., the best of them in lineage and the highest in station; the wasīṭ between disputants; and, like ṣabūr, a verse of poetry, or the smallest of them; the she-camel that fills the vessel; those that carry on their heads and backs, which are not hobbled or tethered; the one that is milked forty days after the year; Wasṭān, a town of the Kurds; Wasaṭ with vowels, a mountain and a circular tract; Wāsiṭ, a place; and wasaṭ with vowels: what lies between its two ends, like awsaṭ; and when given sukūn it is an adverb; or both apply to what is solid like a ring, whereas if its parts are distinct then it is with sukūn only; or every place where 'between' is suitable is with sukūn, and otherwise it is with vowels."
(لَكَنُودٌ) Al-kanūd: the ungrateful. Kanada l-niʿma kunūdan; from it Kinda was named, because he was ungrateful to his father and left him. From al-Kalbī: al-kanūd in the language of Kinda is the disobedient, in the language of Banū Mālik the miserly, and in the language of Muḍar and Rabīʿa the ungrateful. In al-Mukhtār: "Kanada: he was ungrateful for a favour; its pattern is dakhala; so he is kanūd, and a woman is also kanūd." Abū Umāma al-Bāhilī reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Al-kanūd is the one who eats alone, withholds his rifd (his giving), and beats his slave." The wording of Ibn Khālawayh: Al-kanūd is the ungrateful. Al-Ḥasan said on His saying, the Mighty and Exalted, (إن الإنسان لربه لكنود): "He recalls misfortunes and forgets favours." Al-Namir ibn Tawlab said:
كنود لا تمنّ ولا تغادي ... إذا علقت حبائلها برهن
لها ما تشتهي عسل مصفّى ... إذا شاءت وحوّارى بسمن
(Ungrateful, she neither bestows favour nor goes out in the morning, when her ties are fastened to a pledge; she has what she desires, refined honey whenever she wishes, and white flour with ghee.) [Translator's note: the rendering of the first verse is tentative.]
(بُعْثِرَ) Its explanation has often been given before. Al-baʿthara and al-baḥthara with ḥāʾ mean extracting a thing and uncovering it.

* I'rab:
(وَالْعادِياتِ ضَبْحاً فَالْمُورِياتِ قَدْحاً فَالْمُغِيراتِ صُبْحاً) The wāw is a particle of oath and genitive; (العاديات) is genitive by the wāw of oath and the preposition and its genitive noun are attached to the omitted verb of the oath. (ضبحا) is a mafʿūl muṭlaq of an omitted verb, i.e., "they pant a panting", and this implied verb is a ḥāl from (العاديات); it can also be parsed as a ḥāl, i.e., "panting". Al-Khaṭīb said: "The accusative of (ضبحا) is by the implication of a verb, i.e., 'they pant a panting', or by (العاديات), as if it were said 'by the panting ones, panting', because panting occurs only with running; or as ḥāl, i.e., panting." The fāʾ is a conjunction and (الموريات) is conjoined to (العاديات); (قدحا) has the three aspects of (ضبحا). Al-Zamakhsharī said: "(قدحا) is accusative by what (ضبحا) is accusative by." The fāʾ is a conjunction and (المغيرات) is also conjoined to (العاديات); (ضبحا) [Translator's note: the source writes ضبحا here, but the word in the verse is (صبحا)] is accusative as an adverb, i.e., "the ones that raid at the time of morning", and it is attached to (المغيرات). Abū Ḥayyān said, and well: "In this is evidence that these descriptions apply to a single entity, because they are conjoined with the fāʾ, which implies immediate succession. The apparent meaning is that they are the horses on which the disbelieving enemy is fought, and it is not valid to argue that they are camels from the battle of Badr, even though there were only two horsemen in it, since it is not reported that the cause of revelation of this sūra was the battle of Badr; furthermore, it is hardly found that camels were used for jihad in the cause of Allah; rather it is known that jihad in the cause of Allah, the Exalted, is waged only on horses, in the east and west of the lands." He said this in the course of refuting those who interpreted (العاديات) as camels. (فَأَثَرْنَ بِهِ نَقْعاً فَوَسَطْنَ بِهِ جَمْعاً) The fāʾ is a conjunction; (أثرن) is a past verb, indeclinable on sukūn, and the nūn is the fāʿil. The conjunction is on a verb, with the active participle's place being replaced, because the meaning is "and those that ran, then struck fire, then raided, then raised". (به) are two elements attached to (أثرن); (نقعا) is a direct object; and the pronoun in (به) refers to the valley, even though it was not mentioned before, which is the place of running; it is also said that it refers to the morning, i.e., "they raised dust in it at the time of morning". Abū Ḥayyān said: "This is better than the first because it is explicitly mentioned." On either interpretation the bāʾ in (به) means "in", and everything that takes "in" can take the bāʾ, but not the reverse. The fāʾ is a conjunction; (وسطن) is a past verb indeclinable on sukūn and the nūn of the feminine plural is the fāʿil; (به) are two elements attached to (وسطن), the pronoun referring to the morning as above or to the dust, in which case the bāʾ is of transitivity, whereas on the first it is locative. It is also said that the bāʾ is a bāʾ of ḥāl, i.e., "they came into the middle accompanied by dust", so it is attached to an omitted element as ḥāl. Abū l-Baqāʾ reported a strange view for which I found no justification, namely that it is redundant, and (جمعا) is the object of (أثرن); and Abū l-Baqāʾ made it stranger still by making it a ḥāl, because he made the bāʾ redundant in the direct object; it is not so. Regrettably Ibn Khālawayh parsed (جمعا) as an adverb, and I do not know, nor does the astrologer know, how that held up for him. (إِنَّ الْإِنْسانَ لِرَبِّهِ لَكَنُودٌ) The clause has no grammatical position because it is the answer to the oath. (إن) is a particle resembling the verb; (الإنسان) is its noun; (لربه) are two elements attached to (كنود); the lām is the shifted lām (al-lām al-muzaḥlaqa); (كنود) is the khabar of (إن). The alif-lām in (الإنسان) is generic; it is also said to refer to the unbeliever, but the first is preferable, because the nature of man is created that way, calling him to evil, except for whom Allah protects. (وَإِنَّهُ عَلى ذلِكَ لَشَهِيدٌ) Conjoined to the preceding clause, and it is the second thing sworn to. (إن) and its noun; (على ذلك) are two elements attached to (شديد) [Translator's note: the source writes "shadīd" here, but the word in the verse is (شهيد)]; the shifted lām; and (شديد) [sic; (شهيد)] is the khabar of (إن), i.e., he bears witness against himself by what he does, a witness by force that appears in the clear traces of his deeds and their exposing evidences. Al-Zamakhsharī permitted the pronoun to refer to Allah, saying: "It is also said: 'and Allah is, over his ingratitude, a witness', by way of threat." (وَإِنَّهُ لِحُبِّ الْخَيْرِ لَشَدِيدٌ) Conjoined to what precedes, and it is the third thing sworn to. (إن) and its noun; (لحب الخير) are two elements attached to (شديد); the lām is for reinforcement, the meaning being that he is strong and capable in the love of good. One says "he is shadīd for this matter", i.e., capable of it. It is also said that the lām is causal, i.e., "and he, because of the love of wealth, is indeed tight-fisted", and the shifted lām, with (شديد) its khabar. By "good" (khayr) is meant wealth, and the shadīd is the miser, the tight-fisted; one says "so-and-so is shadīd and mutashaddid". Ṭarafa said:
أرى الموت يعتام الكرام ويصطفي ... عقيلة مال الفاحش المتشدّد
(I see death choosing the noble and selecting the choicest of the wealth of the miser, the tight-fisted.)
The wording of Ibn Khālawayh: "Al-khayr here is wealth, as He said, the Exalted: (إن ترك خيرا), i.e., wealth; al-khayr is also horses, in His saying, the Exalted: (إني أحببت حب الخير عن ذكر ربي), meaning horses; and al-khayr is wine: the Arabs say mā ʿindahu khall wa-lā khamr, i.e., neither evil nor good. Al-khayr has the plural khuyūr and al-sharr has shurūr." I say: I did not find in the dictionaries at my disposal this meaning of khayr, i.e., wine, and I would not have recorded this remark, because Ibn Khālawayh is one of the imams attested for retention; but I recorded my remark as a comment on his citing of the proverb. The context in which he cites it indicates that khayr may mean wine, but the proverb certainly does not intend that; rather evil is made vinegar and good wine by way of simile. So their saying in the proverb "he has neither vinegar nor wine" means "he has neither good nor evil", and their saying "you are neither vinegar nor wine" means what al-Maydānī and others pointed out, namely that some Arabs made good "wine" for its pleasantness and evil "vinegar" for its sourness and because a person cannot drink it. (أَفَلا يَعْلَمُ إِذا بُعْثِرَ ما فِي الْقُبُورِ) The hamza is for rebuking interrogation, and the fāʾ is a conjunction on an implied element that the context requires, i.e., "Does he do what he does of vile deeds and not know?" (لا) is negative and (يعلم) is an imperfect verb in the nominative. (إذا) is an adverb for mere time-reference. Zādeh said: "It cannot be an adverb of (يعلم), because knowledge is not what is wanted of man at that time; it is wanted of him while he is in this world. It cannot be an adverb of (بعثر), because the muḍāf ilayhi does not govern the muḍāf; nor of His saying (خبير), because what follows (إن) does not govern what precedes it. So the governing element must be what is indicated by His saying (إن ربهم بهم يومئذ لخبير), i.e., 'Does man not know, in this world, that He, the Exalted, will requite him when it is overturned?' The meaning of Allah's knowledge of them on the Day of Resurrection is His requital of them." The clause (بعثر) is in the position of genitive through the annexation of the adverb to it. (ما) is a relative, the nāʾib fāʿil of (بعثر); (في القبور) are two elements attached to an omitted element with no grammatical position, as the ṣila of (ما). (وَحُصِّلَ ما فِي الصُّدُورِ) Conjoined to (بعثر ما في القبور). (حصل) is a passive past verb, meaning it was gathered in the records and displayed in detail, collected; and it is said: good was distinguished from evil, fat from lean. Zādeh said: "He singled out the deeds of the hearts for mention and omitted the deeds of the limbs, because they follow the deeds of the hearts; for were the motives and intentions not realised in the hearts, the acts of the limbs would not come about." This is a good statement, so ponder it. (إِنَّ رَبَّهُمْ بِهِمْ يَوْمَئِذٍ لَخَبِيرٌ) The clause is a justification for the omitted governor of (إذا), which is the object of (يعلم), i.e., "Does he not know that We will requite him at the time mentioned?" Then He justified that by His saying "Indeed their Lord..." etc. (إن) and its noun; (بهم) are two elements attached to (خبير); (يومئذ) is an adverb also attached to (خبير); the shifted lām; and (خبير) is the khabar of (إن).

* Rhetoric:
1- In the difference between the conjoined and the thing it is conjoined to in His saying «فأثرن به نقعا», in that a verb is conjoined to the noun that is (العاديات) and what follows it — because those are active participles that give the meaning of a verb — there is a wonderful secret: the depiction of these actions in the soul and their embodiment before the eye. For depiction is achieved by bringing a verb after a noun, because of the contrast between them, and it is more eloquent than depiction and embodiment by harmonious nouns. Likewise the depiction by an imperfect after a past, for which there have been examples, the closest being the saying of ʿAmr ibn Maʿdī Karib:
بأني قد لقيت الغول تهوي ... بسهب كالصحيفة صحصحان
فأضربها بلا دهش فخرت ... صريعا لليدين وللجران
(That I met the ghoul swooping down upon a plain like a sheet, level and open; / I struck her without bewilderment, and she fell, prostrate on her hands and her neck.)
2- In His saying «فالموريات قدحا» there is a metaphor for the horses kindling war; it is an explicit metaphor (istiʿāra taṣrīḥiyya): war is likened to a blazing fire, the likened is omitted and the likened-to is retained. The Exalted said: (كلما أوقدوا نارا للحرب أطفأها الله), and it is said "ḥamiya l-waṭīs" (the oven grew hot) when war intensifies.
3- In His saying «إن ربهم بهم يومئذ لخبير» there is tajnīs al-taḥrīf (paronomasia of altered vowelling), which some call "al-jinās al-muḥarraf", which is where the vowel-pointing is what distinguishes the two words or parts of them; it is also what has its two members agreeing in number of letters and differing in vowels, whether they are from two nouns, two verbs, a noun and a verb, or other. The utmost of it is His saying, the Exalted: (ولقد أرسلنا فيهم منذرين، فانظر كيف كان عاقبة المنذرين). It is not said that the two words are identical in meaning so that there is no paronomasia between them, because we say that the first is meant as active participle and the second as passive participle, so the difference is clear. Of it is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "O Allah, as You have made my khalq (form) good, make my khuluq (character) good", and similar to it their saying jubbat al-burd, junnat al-burd, and their saying raṭib al-ruṭab, ḍarb min al-ḍarb. Of poetry is the saying of Abū Tammām:
هنّ الحمام فإن كسرت عيافة ... من خائهنّ فإنهنّ حمام
(They are doves [ḥamām]; if you break off the omen-reading from their "khāʾ", then they are death [ḥimām].) [Translator's note: the rendering of this verse is tentative.]
and similarly the saying of al-Maʿarrī:
والحسن يظهر في شيئين رونقه ... بيت من الشعر أو بيت من الشعر
(Beauty shows its brilliance in two things: a house of hair [a tent] or a verse of poetry.)
and from him also:
لغيري زكاة من جمال فإن تكن ... زكاة جمال فاذكري ابن سبيل
(For others the alms [tax] of beauty; if there is an alms of beauty, then remember the wayfarer.)
4- In His saying «وإنه على ذلك لشهيد وإنه لحب الخير لشديد» there is al-jinās al-lāḥiq, which is where one of its two members has one letter replaced by another not of the same articulation point, whether the replacement is at the beginning, middle or end; if what is replaced is of the same articulation point it is called muḍāriʿ. An example of replacement at the beginning is His saying, the Exalted: (ويل لكل همزة لمزة); the verse we are on is an example of replacement in the middle; and an example of replacement at the end is His saying, the Exalted: (وإذا جاءهم أمر من الأمن). Among ḥadīths of this type, from the beginning is his saying, peace be upon him: "Praise be to Allah who made my form good and adorned in me what disfigured in others"; from the second, the ḥadīth of al-Ṭabarānī, "Were it not for bowing men, suckling infants and grazing beasts"; and from the third, also al-Ṭabarānī's ḥadīth, "My community will not perish until there appear among them al-tamāyuz and al-tamāyul", and al-Daylamī's ḥadīth, "The most beloved of believers to Allah is the one who devotes himself to obedience to Allah and gives sincere counsel to the community of Muḥammad". Among poetic examples in the same order, also, is the saying of Abū Firās:
إن الغني هو الغني بنفسه ... ولو أنه عاري المناكب حافي
ما كل ما فوق البسيطة كافيا ... وإذا قنعت فكل شيء كافي
(True wealth is wealth of the self, even if one is bare-shouldered and barefoot. Not everything on the face of the earth suffices; but when you are content, everything suffices.)
and from the second, the saying of al-Buḥturī:
وقعودي عن التقلب والأر ... ض لمثلي رحيبة الأكناف
ليس عن ثروة بلغت مداها ... غير أنّي امرؤ كفاني كفافي
(My sitting back from roving, though the earth is wide-flanked for one like me, is not from wealth that has reached its limit, but because I am a man whom my sufficiency suffices.)
and from the third, the saying of one of them:
شوقي لذاك المحيا الزاهر الزاهي ... شوق شديد وجسمي الواهن الواهي
أسهرت طرفي وولهت الفؤاد هوى ... فالقلب والطرف بين الساهر الساهي
(My longing for that radiant, shining face is intense longing, and my body is weak and frail. Love has kept my eye awake and driven my heart distraught; so heart and eye are between one wakeful and one heedless.)
